newsitem.title: SLOVAKIA: Slovak c.bank extends crown support through fix.
newsitem.headline: Slovak c.bank extends crown support through fix.

text.p: The National Bank of Slovakia (NBS), for the fourth consecutive day, fixed the crown stronger than market levels on Thursday sticking to its commitment to support the currency which has been under pressure.
The NBS fixed the crown at 33.230 to the dollar and at 19.616 to the mark, implying a deviation of -0.78 percent versus the mark/dollar basket parity.
The crown was trading at -1.46 percent versus the midpoint at the time of the late morning fixing calculation.

"It seems that the NBS is really committed to continue in supporting the crown by using its market tools both on the forex market and the local interbank market," said one Bratislava-based foreign bank trader.
He said the NBS fixing gave the local banks an opportunity to complement their hard currency positions and prevented the crown from coming under even stronger downward pressure.

Dusan Svitek, an FX trader of Slovenska Sporitelna, estimated the volume of crowns NBS had to buy at its fixing this week at some $350 million. The NBS hard currency reserves stood at $3.398 billion as of May 14.

"Furthermore, the NBS is carrying out a wise strategy on the local money market by keeping it short of liquidity and thus limiting access to crown funds which should be converted to hard currencies and spark a run on the crown," the dealer said.

Short-term rates on the Slovak interbank market jumped to a record 44 percent on Thursday morning and traders said local banks stopped quoting crown deposit rates due to an acute liquidity shortage on the market.
Traders said the market was short of some six billion crowns against the minimum reserve requirement, adding that the NBS seemed determined not to add excessive liquidity.
Some traders said the NBS appeared unlikely to copy the Czech central bank's administrative moves to curb lending activities for foreign banks to limit access to crown funds.
"The NBS looks like it wanted the high money market to limit access to crown funds and thus prevent pressure on the crown," said Martin Hrozany of Credit Lyonnais Bank.

"I think the (Slovak) central bank wants to use its market tools to push local commercial banks to stop lending crowns and selling hard currencies to foreign banks so that it (NBS) should not impose any administrative measures." Hrozany added.
Vladimir Kuklis of CSOB bank said he did not see macroeconomic fundamentals behind the run on the Slovak crown.

But Kuklis warned that close connection between the Czech and Slovak currencies could bring fears that if the Czech Republic is pushed to actively devalue its currency, Slovakia would have to follow with a similar move.
"I think that Slovaks would have to follow if Prague decides to devalue the Czech crown by more than 10 percent," Kuklis said.
